opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was really one of the key moves going from attribution-based parameter decomposition, APD, to stochastic parameter decomposition. In APD, each parameter component was essentially a full copy of the model's parameters, a whole vector in parameter space the same size as the network. That was conceptually clean, but it was really expensive. If you want thousands of components, you're storing thousands of copies of the model, and it made scaling very hard.

So in SPD, instead of components that span the whole network, we decompose each weight matrix separately into a sum of rank-one matrices, each an outer product of two vectors, a U and a V. We call these subcomponents. That's dramatically cheaper in memory and compute, because you're storing two vectors rather than a full matrix, let alone a full model.

There's also a nice conceptual reason. A rank-one matrix is about the simplest computational unit a linear layer can implement: it reads from one direction in the input space and writes to one direction in the output space. So you're breaking the network's mechanisms down into tiny atoms of computation. If a real mechanism needs more than rank one, say it spans several layers or needs a higher-rank transformation, then you can recover it by grouping subcomponents that tend to activate together. You build the bigger mechanisms out of rank-one pieces rather than assuming their shape up front.

And it helped optimization a lot. With APD we had a top-k selection of components and had to tune hyperparameters carefully, and it was quite brittle. With rank-one subcomponents plus learned causal importance values and stochastic masking, where we sample masks between the importance value and one and require the model output to stay the same, the whole thing became much more stable. The stochastic part pushes the model to say which subcomponents can be ablated without changing the output, and the rank-one structure keeps that tractable.

There are tradeoffs, of course. Rank-one is a strong assumption at the level of individual pieces, and there's real work in figuring out how to cluster those pieces into faithful higher-level mechanisms, especially across layers. But as a basic unit, it's let us scale the method to much bigger models than APD could reach, and the decompositions we get look quite interpretable on the toy models where we know the ground truth.

r001.rationale: It contrasts full-model APD components with per-weight-matrix rank-one subcomponents, explicitly describing the shift to smaller units.

r002.rationale: It says higher-rank transformations can be recovered by grouping rank-one subcomponents.

r003.rationale: It says mechanisms spanning several layers can be recovered by grouping subcomponents that activate together.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the core move in SPD, and it's worth motivating it from where we were before. In the earlier work, Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition, we were decomposing the model's parameters into components that were full-rank matrices, each the same shape as the original weight matrix. That was clean conceptually, but it had a few practical problems. The memory cost scaled terribly, you had to store a whole copy of the weights for every component, and the optimization was unstable in ways that were hard to diagnose. And there was this nasty failure mode where a single component could end up being a kind of "junk drawer" that absorbed lots of unrelated mechanisms, because nothing really stopped it from doing so.

The idea in stochastic parameter decomposition is to say: let's just restrict each component to be rank one. So each component is an outer product of two vectors, a u and a v, for each weight matrix in the network. The full matrix is then the sum over all these rank-one pieces. At first glance that sounds like a big limitation, because the mechanisms we actually care about in networks are clearly not all rank one. But the trick is that you don't have to identify one component with one mechanism. A mechanism can be a group of rank-one subcomponents that happen to get used together. So you've moved the "grouping" from being baked into the parameterization to being something that emerges from the training signal, and you can read it off afterwards by looking at which subcomponents co-activate.

And there are a couple of reasons that turns out to be a really nice thing to do. One is that rank one is a very strong inductive bias toward minimality. A single rank-one matrix basically can't be a junk drawer, there's not enough room in it. So that pathology where one component swallows everything just largely goes away. The other is that it makes the whole thing much more tractable. You have far fewer parameters to store, and the optimization is just better behaved. We could scale it to things we couldn't touch with the earlier method.

The "stochastic" part of the name comes in because, once you have these subcomponents, you need some way of asking "which ones are actually causally needed on this input?" In APD we used attribution methods for that, gradient-times-activation style estimates, and that was both noisy and sort of philosophically unsatisfying because attributions are approximations. In SPD we instead learn a causal importance for each subcomponent on each input, and then we train by randomly ablating subcomponents in proportion to how unimportant they're predicted to be and checking that the output doesn't change. So you're directly optimizing for the property you want, that unimportant components can be removed without affecting behavior, rather than relying on a proxy.

So to put it together: rank one is the thing that makes components cheap, minimal, and resistant to the junk-drawer problem; the stochastic masking is the thing that gives you a principled way to decide which of those tiny pieces matter on each input; and the mechanisms you care about are the clusters of rank-one pieces that get recruited together. I think of it less as "we've assumed mechanisms are rank one" and more as "we've picked a basis fine enough that any mechanism can be expressed as a union of pieces, and then we let the data tell us the groupings."

r001.rationale: It describes replacing full-matrix components with rank-one pieces for each weight matrix, making the representation finer-grained.

r002.rationale: It says mechanisms that are not rank one can be represented as groups or unions of rank-one subcomponents.

r003.rationale: It does not state that rank-one units from different layers can be grouped to recover a component spanning multiple layers.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that a rank-one matrix gives you a much smaller building block. You can write it as an outer product of two vectors: one picks out a direction in the incoming activations, and the other tells you which direction to write to in the output. Then you approximate a weight matrix as a sum of those contributions.

In stochastic parameter decomposition, you can put stochastic gates on those contributions and ask which ones you need to retain to preserve the model’s behavior. Compared with giving each component a full matrix of parameters, that imposes a much stronger structural constraint and makes each component cheaper to represent.

But there’s a distinction between a convenient unit of parameterization and a meaningful unit of computation. A rank-one contribution isn’t automatically an interpretable feature or a circuit. A meaningful computation might require several of them, potentially across layers. So the appeal is that you get finer-grained building blocks; the challenge is figuring out how those building blocks fit together into something that actually explains the model.

r001.rationale: It describes each rank-one contribution as a smaller building block and contrasts it with giving each component a full matrix.

r002.rationale: It says meaningful computations may require several rank-one contributions, but does not state that higher-rank parameter components can be recovered post hoc by grouping them.

r003.rationale: It mentions computations across layers, but does not state that multi-layer parameter components can be recovered post hoc by grouping rank-one units.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that a rank-one matrix gives you a very simple building block: it reads out one direction in the input and writes along one direction in the output. You can express a weight matrix as a sum of those building blocks, and then ask which ones need to be present to preserve the model’s behavior.

In stochastic parameter decomposition, the important part is that you’re randomly dropping components during training. That puts pressure on the decomposition to organize the computation into components that are useful and selectively necessary, rather than just finding an arbitrary factorization of the weights.

The attraction of rank-one components is that they’re much smaller and more constrained than a component containing a whole model’s worth of parameters. But there’s a tradeoff: a meaningful computation might require several rank-one pieces working together, potentially across multiple layers. So I wouldn’t assume that each rank-one matrix corresponds to a human-understandable concept. It’s a building block for finding the computational structure, and whether that structure is interpretable is something we have to test.

r001.rationale: It describes rank-one matrices as smaller building blocks and dropping components during training, but does not clearly state that full-model parameter components are presplit into single-layer units.

r002.rationale: It does not say that higher-rank components can be recovered afterward by grouping rank-one units.

r003.rationale: It mentions computations using several rank-one pieces across layers, but not recovering multi-layer components post hoc by grouping those units.
